name: C-arm Flat-Detector CT Parenchymal Blood Volume maps
description: C-arm flat-detector computed tomography (FDCT) parenchymal blood volume (PBV) maps are an imaging technique used to estimate blood volume within brain tissue. A C-arm angiography system captures rotational images before and during intravenous contrast administration. The images are then processed to generate voxel-based maps of parenchymal blood volume. Following aSAH, areas of substantially reduced PBV may indicate severely ischemic or infarcted brain tissue.
reference_1: Kamran M and Byrne JV. C-Arm Flat Detector CT Parenchymal Blood Volume Thresholds for Identification of Infarcted Parenchyma in the Neurointerventional Suite. AJNR Am J Neuroradiol 2015; 36(9): 1748-55. https://doi.org/10.3174/ajnr.A4339

name: Negative ultraslow potential
description: A negative ultraslow potential (NUP) is a large, prolonged negative shift in the brain's electrical potential that can occur when brain cells progressively lose their ability to recover from ischemic injury. As the injury becomes irreversible, brain cells die and tissue damage accumulates. NUP can be detected through continuous electrocorticography (ECoG), using electrodes placed directly on the surface of the brain. Following aSAH, NUP has been proposed as an electrophysiological marker of irreversible brain tissue injury and developing cerebral infarction, potentially identifying infarction while it is evolving rather than only after it becomes visible on conventional imaging.
reference_1: Lückl J, Lemale CL, Kola V, et al. The negative ultraslow potential, electrophysiological correlate of infarction in the human cortex. Brain 2018; 141(6): 1734-1752. https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/awy102

name: Non-contrast computed tomography
description: Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) is an X-ray imaging technique performed without intravenous contrast material. Cerebral infarction can appear on CT images as an area of reduced tissue density. Following aSAH, CT can be used to identify the presence, location, and extent of cerebral infarction
reference_1: Vergouwen MDI, Vermeulen M, van Gijn J, et al. Definition of delayed cerebral ischemia after aneurysmal sub-arachnoid hemorrhage as an outcome event in clinical trials and observational studies: proposal of a multidisciplinary research group. Stroke 2010; 41: 2391–5. https://doi.org/10.1161/STROKEAHA.110.589275

name: Magnetic Resonance Imaging
description: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an imaging technique that uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to produce detailed images of the brain. Different MRI sequences, such as diffusion-weighted imaging, can be used to identify changes in brain tissue associated with cerebral infarction. Following aSAH, MRI can be used to identify the presence, location, and extent of cerebral infarction.
